predictions.title: Inline MCP-channel policy enforcement ships as a platform default by Q1 2027
predictions.body: At Zenith Live 2026 on June 9, Zscaler announced AI Broker, which it positions as the industry's first product that sits inline on MCP and agent-to-agent (A2A) channels and enforces per-agent scoped access at the network layer — not at the application layer — so that no agent call traverses the network without an explicit policy approval. On the same week, Databricks' Agent Bricks (announced June 16 at Data + AI Summit) independently embedded MCP integration with Unity Catalog, letting enterprise teams write contextual security policies in SQL that govern which agents may access which data sources via MCP. Two unrelated production platforms converging on the same design in a single week is the structural signal: inline MCP-channel access control is hardening from a post-hoc add-on (a proxy you bolt on after the agent is built) into a platform default (a policy engine the agent runtime calls before any tool invocation leaves the process boundary). The forward thesis is that this pattern — MCP-channel policy enforcement as a first-class runtime default rather than a perimeter add-on — propagates into a second major agent platform beyond the two already shipping it. The concrete, falsifiable landing: by Q1 2027 (on or before 2027-03-31) a third major agent platform or cloud provider's agent runtime — distinct from Zscaler's Zero Trust Exchange and Databricks' Agent Bricks — ships documented, production-ready MCP-channel inline policy enforcement (per-agent scoped access, not just network-perimeter filtering) as a default or first-class feature, with a public product page or GA announcement. What does NOT count: a bolt-on third-party proxy marketed as an add-on integration; a closed beta or preview with no documented GA path; a platform that enforces access at the application layer only (e.g. prompt guards or output filters) rather than at the MCP channel level; a vendor announcement with no shipped product. If by March 31, 2027 only Zscaler and Databricks offer inline MCP-channel policy enforcement as a default capability in their agent runtimes, the prediction fails.

reasoning.because: Zscaler AI Broker (June 9) and Databricks Agent Bricks (June 16) both ship inline MCP-channel policy enforcement as a default
reasoning.given: two unrelated platforms converging on the same design in one week signals a hardening pattern, not a coincidence
reasoning.so_that: a third major agent platform or cloud provider ships inline MCP-channel access control as a production default by Q1 2027
reasoning.landing: by Q1 2027 (2027-03): 3rd platform GA with inline MCP-channel policy enforcement
reasoning.plain_language: Two big AI platforms just made it so AI agents can't talk to outside tools without permission checks; soon a third major platform will do the same.

predictions.summary: Zscaler and Databricks independently shipped inline MCP-channel policy enforcement as a production default in the same week, signaling the pattern is hardening from a bolt-on add-on into a platform expectation. A third major agent platform or cloud provider is predicted to ship the same capability as a first-class default by Q1 2027.

predictions.title: OpenSharing becomes the default cross-org AI-asset sharing protocol by Q3 2027
predictions.body: On June 10, Databricks and the Linux Foundation announced OpenSharing, a vendor-neutral open protocol extending Delta Sharing to cover agent skills, AI models, and unstructured data, enabling zero-copy cross-organizational sharing of AI assets without proprietary marketplaces. The founding partner roster is commercially significant: OpenAI, SAP, Stripe, Atlassian, and Amadeus. This is not a niche data-engineering standard — it places OpenSharing squarely at the intersection of enterprise SaaS (SAP, Atlassian), payments infrastructure (Stripe), and frontier model providers (OpenAI). The business thesis is that these founding partners anchor a network-effect dynamic: each enterprise that adopts OpenSharing to share agent skills with a partner avoids building a bespoke point-to-point integration, which in turn reduces the switching cost of choosing OpenSharing-compatible vendors. Historically, vendor-neutral protocols backed by a major cloud data incumbent (Databricks) plus a neutral foundation (Linux Foundation) and a critical mass of SaaS leaders move from launch to de-facto standard in 12-24 months when the use case has obvious bilateral demand — file formats (Parquet), table formats (Delta, Iceberg), and container runtimes (OCI) followed this arc. The concrete, falsifiable landing: by Q3 2027 at least three additional Fortune 500 SaaS or cloud vendors publicly announce OpenSharing compatibility or integrations — documented in a Databricks or Linux Foundation press release, a GitHub merge to the official OpenSharing spec, or a named announcement at a data or AI conference. What does NOT count: individual customer implementations without vendor-level commitment; integrations built on Delta Sharing alone without the OpenSharing AI-asset extension; non-Fortune-500 adopters; or 'coming soon' roadmap items without a generally available implementation. The counter-risk is that hyperscalers (AWS, Microsoft, Google) each back competing proprietary asset-sharing surfaces, fragmenting the market and preventing OpenSharing from crossing the critical SaaS-partnership threshold.

reasoning.because: Databricks + Linux Foundation launched OpenSharing June 10 with OpenAI, SAP, Stripe, Atlassian, Amadeus as founding partners
reasoning.given: Vendor-neutral protocols backed by a major platform + neutralfoundation + SaaS leaders reach de-facto status within 12-24 months
reasoning.so_that: By Q3 2027 three or more additional Fortune 500 SaaS or cloud vendors ship OpenSharing-compatible integrations
reasoning.landing: by Q3 2027: three or more additional Fortune 500 vendors announce OpenSharing compatibility
reasoning.plain_language: Big companies joined a new open standard for sharing AI tools, so it will likely become the go-to way companies share AI with each other.

predictions.summary: Databricks and the Linux Foundation launched OpenSharing on June 10 with founding partners including OpenAI, SAP, Stripe, and Atlassian — a vendor-neutral protocol for sharing agent skills, AI models, and data across organizations. The combination of a major data platform, a neutral foundation, and enterprise SaaS leaders mirrors the adoption arc of Parquet and Delta. By Q3 2027 at least three additional Fortune 500 vendors should publicly commit to OpenSharing compatibility.

predictions.title: US export-control regime gains a defensive-cyber AI carve-out by Q1 2027
predictions.body: The June 12 directive suspending Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos 5 — triggered by a claimed jailbreak technique involving asking the model to read a codebase and fix software flaws — has exposed a structural gap in current export-control doctrine. As security researcher Katie Moussouris noted on June 16, the flagged capability is precisely the most valuable task an AI model can perform for cyber defense, and the same capability is present in competing systems including GPT-5.5. Anthropic has explicitly stated that applying a narrow jailbreak-equals-recall standard uniformly across the industry would effectively halt all new frontier model deployments. The live Washington negotiation — unusual in its speed, with senior Anthropic technical staff dispatched and at least some officials signaling openness to a technical compromise — is establishing a forcing function: any negotiated resolution must either define a defensible bright line between offensive and defensive code-fixing use, or grant an explicit defensive-security carve-out. The prediction is that this episode produces a durable policy artifact. By Q1 2027 (March 2027), expect the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, a Congressional committee, or a formal NIST/CISA guidance document to publish criteria distinguishing permissible defensive-security AI capabilities from recall-triggering offensive ones. What counts: a published federal document (rule, guidance, or committee report) that explicitly names AI-assisted vulnerability remediation or code analysis as a recognized defensive-use category with defined boundary conditions. What does NOT count: an informal statement from a government spokesperson, a single-company negotiated license exemption, a court order, or an industry white paper with no federal imprimatur.

reasoning.because: US suspended Fable 5/Mythos 5 over a jailbreak touching the same code-analysis capability used for cyber defense
reasoning.given: Any negotiated resolution must define a bright line between offensive and defensive AI code-fixing to be durable
reasoning.so_that: Federal policy acquires explicit defensive-security carve-out criteria, preventing uniform jailbreak-recall from blocking all frontier deployments
reasoning.landing: by Q1 2027 (March 2027): BIS, Congress, or NIST/CISA publishes defensive-AI boundary criteria
reasoning.plain_language: The US government banned an AI model for a hacking risk, but the same feature helps defend computers, so officials will write rules to tell the difference.

predictions.summary: The June 12 suspension of Fable 5 and Mythos 5 over a jailbreak involving code analysis — a core defensive-security capability also present in GPT-5.5 — forces a policy resolution that cannot simply recall every model with code-fixing ability. The live Washington negotiation is the fastest-moving forcing function for a formal federal carve-out distinguishing permissible defensive AI code analysis from recall-triggering offensive use. By Q1 2027, expect BIS, a Congressional committee, or NIST/CISA to publish explicit boundary criteria for defensive-security AI capabilities.
